:::{.callout-tip}
This post is part of the [Agentic Development Series](index.qmd). It follows on
from [Part 7 — agent-to-agent interoperability with A2A](07-a2a-interoperability.qmd).
:::

Every agent in this series so far is a frozen large model plus a prompt. That's
the right way to start, but it has a real cost once you're running an agent
thousands of times a day: every call pays full inference cost and full latency
on a large model, even for decisions that turn out to be fairly routine, like
"is this void ratio within the normal range." I already treat distillation as a
compounding strategic asset in my own work, more valuable the longer a system
runs, and this post is that same logic applied to an agent's decisions instead
of a vision model's weights.

The core idea: run the large, expensive model on real traffic for a while, log
every input and every good output, then fine-tune a much smaller model on
those logged pairs, so the small model learns to reproduce the large model's
specific decisions for your specific task, without the large model's general-
purpose overhead.

## Jargon, explained simply

**Distillation.** Training a smaller model to imitate a larger model's
outputs, rather than training it from scratch on the original task.

**Teacher model.** The larger model whose outputs you're using as training
data.

**Student model.** The smaller model being trained to imitate the teacher.

**LoRA.** Low-rank adaptation, a way to fine-tune a model by training a small
number of extra weights, instead of updating every weight in the model, which
is why it fits on a single GPU.

**Held-out set.** Data kept aside during training, never seen by the model, so
you can evaluate honestly instead of grading on data it already memorized.

**Staged rollout.** Gradually increasing what fraction of real traffic a new
model handles, instead of switching everything over at once.

## Step one: instrument my agent to log training pairs

I already have most of this from the observability section in [part
six](06-advanced-agentic-development.qmd). I extend it slightly so every agent
call also writes a clean input, output pair to a dataset file, not just a
trace span.

```python
import json
import os

DISTILLATION_LOG = "distillation_pairs.jsonl"


def log_distillation_pair(agent_name: str, input_messages: list, output_text: str):
    record = {
        "agent": agent_name,
        "messages": input_messages,
        "output": output_text,
    }
    with open(DISTILLATION_LOG, "a") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")


def traced_agent_call_with_logging(client, agent_name, model, messages, **kwargs):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=messages, **kwargs)
    output_text = response.choices[0].message.content
    log_distillation_pair(agent_name, messages, output_text)
    return response
```

Run my error-analysis agent this way for a few weeks against real production
traffic, and `distillation_pairs.jsonl` fills up with exactly the input and
output pairs I need, no separate data-collection effort, since it's piggy-
backing on traffic I was already generating anyway.

## Step two: filter for quality before training on anything

Not every logged pair is a good training example, some were wrong, some were
later overridden by a human through the HITL queue from part six. Filter these
out before training, this one step matters more than almost anything else in
the whole process.

```python
def filter_high_quality_pairs(raw_pairs_path, hitl_queue_path):
    with open(hitl_queue_path) as f:
        hitl_queue = json.load(f)

    overridden_outputs = {
        ticket["context"].get("original_output")
        for ticket in hitl_queue.values()
        if ticket["status"] == "resolved" and ticket["resolution"] != "approved"
    }

    clean_pairs = []
    with open(raw_pairs_path) as f:
        for line in f:
            record = json.loads(line)
            if record["output"] not in overridden_outputs:
                clean_pairs.append(record)
    return clean_pairs
```

Any case a human later corrected should never be used as a positive training
example, that would just teach the small model to repeat the same mistake with
more confidence.

## Step three: fine-tune a small model on the filtered data

Given my own hardware, a local Qwen3 model is a natural distillation target, I
already have the serving infrastructure via vLLM. The general recipe, using
LoRA so this is realistic on a single GPU:

```python
from datasets import Dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TrainingArguments, Trainer
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

model_name = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name)

lora_config = LoraConfig(
    r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj"],
)
model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config)


def format_example(record):
    prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(record["messages"], tokenize=False)
    full_text = prompt + record["output"]
    return {"text": full_text}


clean_pairs = filter_high_quality_pairs("distillation_pairs.jsonl", "hitl_queue.json")
dataset = Dataset.from_list(clean_pairs).map(format_example)


def tokenize(example):
    return tokenizer(example["text"], truncation=True, max_length=2048)


tokenized_dataset = dataset.map(tokenize)

training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./error-analysis-distilled",
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    learning_rate=2e-4,
    logging_steps=10,
    save_strategy="epoch",
)

trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=training_args, train_dataset=tokenized_dataset)
trainer.train()
```

I'm training a four billion parameter model here to imitate a much larger
model's specific decisions on my specific error-analysis task, not to be
generally smart. That narrowness is exactly what makes distillation work.

## Step four: evaluate the distilled model against the teacher

Before this replaces the large model in production, I run it through the same
component eval from [part four](04-evaluation-error-analysis.qmd), comparing
the small model's decisions against the large model's on a held-out set it
never trained on.

```python
def compare_teacher_student(teacher_client, student_client, held_out_pairs):
    agreements = 0
    for record in held_out_pairs:
        teacher_output = record["output"]
        student_response = student_client.chat.completions.create(
            model="local:error-analysis-distilled",
            messages=record["messages"],
        )
        student_output = student_response.choices[0].message.content

        if student_output.strip().lower()[:20] == teacher_output.strip().lower()[:20]:
            agreements += 1

    agreement_rate = agreements / len(held_out_pairs)
    return {"agreement_rate": agreement_rate, "n": len(held_out_pairs)}
```

A crude prefix match is a starting point, in practice I'd use a proper
LLM-as-judge comparison here, similar to the plausibility judge from part four,
scoring whether the two decisions actually mean the same thing, not just
whether the text matches.

## Step five: roll it out gradually, not all at once

I would not flip one hundred percent of traffic to the distilled model on day
one. Route a small percentage of real traffic to the small model, log both the
small model's decision and what the large model would have said side by side,
and only increase the percentage once the held-out agreement rate has held
steady across real production traffic, not just the original test set.

```python
import random

DISTILLED_TRAFFIC_PERCENT = 10

def route_error_analysis_call(client, messages):
    if random.randint(1, 100) <= DISTILLED_TRAFFIC_PERCENT:
        model = "local:error-analysis-distilled"
    else:
        model = "openai:gpt-4o-mini"
    return client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=messages)
```

Increase `DISTILLED_TRAFFIC_PERCENT` gradually, the same staged-rollout
discipline I'd use for any model change touching a production line, not just
an agentic one.

## Why this is a compounding asset, not a one-off project

Every week the agent runs against real traffic, `distillation_pairs.jsonl`
grows, which means the next distilled model trains on more, and better-
filtered, data than the last one. This is exactly the reasoning behind treating
distillation as a compounding strategic asset rather than a single fine-tuning
exercise, the value keeps growing the longer the system runs, which is very
different economics than simply paying for a bigger model every time a better
one ships.
